target_customer: Mobile phone users and small merchants in Senegal and other West African countries who send, receive and pay with mobile money
problem: Mobile money in francophone West Africa charged high fees, with incumbent rates cited at roughly 3 to 10 percent, making everyday transfers and cash in and out expensive.
business_model: Mobile money with flat low fees, a 1 percent send fee and free deposits and withdrawals, plus merchant and bill payments
product_category: Mobile money and payments in Africa

founders.name: Drew Durbin
previous_startups: Sendwave (remittance app, acquired by WorldRemit, reported 500M deal)

founders.name: Lincoln Quirk
previous_startups: Sendwave (remittance app, acquired by WorldRemit, reported 500M deal)

competitors.name: Orange Money
competitors.what: Telco led mobile money, dominant in Senegal

competitors.name: Free Money (formerly Tigo Cash)
competitors.what: Telco mobile money service in Senegal

technical_complexity.rationale: Mobile money needed a reliable ledger, agent network tooling, USSD or app flows and compliance, standard fintech engineering with heavy operational work for a small team.

defensibility.rationale: A dense agent network, a license to issue e-money and low cost operations were hard for a new entrant to match, though telcos could cut fees as Orange did.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Orange cut its fees to 1 percent in Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire after Wave arrived, but Wave still became the largest operator in Senegal by its own claims.

market_need_then: Orange Money fees were cited at 3 to 10 percent, and many people relied on cash. Wave launched in Senegal in February 2018 with no cash in or out fees and a flat 1 percent send fee.

branding.domain_note: Uses the exact domain wave.com per the company site.

identity.visual_style: Bright sky blue kiosks, signage and branded motorbikes
identity.voice_and_tone: Confident, simple and price led, with casual customer testimonials

branding.brand_signature: Sky blue agent kiosks with a penguin logo
branding.community_and_virality: Press describes sky blue kiosks and motorbikes as a common sight in Senegal. No fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Distinct blue and penguin look visible on the street in Senegal, but sources tie growth mainly to the 1 percent fee.

pivots.why: Founders saw that domestic transfers were also very expensive, and spun Wave out of the Sendwave ecosystem

outcome_analysis: Wave spun out of the Sendwave team and launched in Senegal in 2018 with flat low fees against telco mobile money that charged far more. It became francophone Africa's first unicorn with a 200 million dollar Series A in 2021 at 1.7 billion dollars, held an e-money license and later raised debt. Its fee advantage forced Orange to cut prices, yet it still grew, helped by an agent network and founders with prior startup experience.
notes: The YC directory lists batch Winter 2012 but founding 2018, because the YC batch belongs to the founders earlier company Sendwave. Wave itself was spun out of Sendwave, and sources disagree on whether building began in 2016 or 2018. Seed of about 13.8 million dollars from founders, Founders Fund and Stripe is reported but the CEO declined to confirm, so it is unverified and left out. Sendwave buyer is reported as WorldRemit, year 2020 or 2021 by different sources. An IFC led debt round of about 92 million dollars appears undated. The competitor sources are 2022 retrospectives about 2018 conditions, not contemporaneous. A report of a further 10 million in 2022 is unconfirmed.
